6 Creating Text with R In a clinical Top-Line Results Report, much of the narrative consists of sentences derived directly from analysis datasets: how many subjects were enrolled, what the demographic profile looked like, which adverse events were most frequent. Traditionally these numbers are read from tables and typed into a Word document by hand — a process that is slow, error-prone, and must be repeated every time the data changes. RapTLR provides a set of text-generation functions that produce ready-to-insert narrative strings directly from your R datasets. Each function targets a specific, recurring reporting need: fct_smpl_rest() — report a subject count (with optional percentage) for any filtered population fct_var_text() — describe the distribution of a categorical variable as a formatted list fct_var_text_group() — describe the distribution of a categorical variable per-group breakdown as a formatted list fct_bsl_stats() — summarise a continuous baseline variable with central tendency and spread fct_mst_aes() — identify and describe the most common treatment-emergent adverse events The outputs are plain character strings, so they slot directly into textReplace() to populate placeholders in your Word shell document. All examples in this chapter use the two built-in datasets: library(RapTLR) data("tlr_adsl") # Subject-level analysis dataset (ADSL) — 254 subjects data("tlr_adae") # Adverse events analysis dataset (ADAE) 6.1 fct_smpl_rest() 6.1.1 Purpose fct_smpl_rest() counts rows in a dataset and returns the result as a formatted character string. Two optional filter expressions can be chained: the first (arg_fl_rest) defines the reference population used as the denominator for percentage calculations, and the second (arg_var_rest) defines the subgroup to count as the numerator. 6.1.2 Parameters Parameter Type Default Description arg_dataset data frame — Dataset to filter and count arg_text_desc character "" Text prepended before the count arg_text_end character "" Text appended after the count arg_fl_rest expression — First filter — defines the denominator population arg_var_rest expression — Second filter — defines the subgroup to count arg_lbl character "nbr" Output format: "nbr", "pct", or "nbr-pct" 6.1.3 Examples Example 1 — Total number of subjects fct_smpl_rest(arg_dataset = tlr_adsl) [1] "254" Example 2 — Count within a population flag fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_fl_rest = SAFFL == "Y" ) [1] "254" Example 3 — Embed the count in a sentence fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_text_desc = "This study enrolled ", arg_text_end = " participants in the safety population.", arg_fl_rest = SAFFL == "Y" ) [1] "This study enrolled 254 participants in the safety population." Example 4 — Subgroup count within a population The denominator is the safety population (254); the numerator is subjects assigned to Xanomeline High Dose (84). fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_fl_rest = SAFFL == "Y", arg_var_rest = ARM == "Xanomeline High Dose" ) [1] "84" Example 5 — Return as a percentage fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_fl_rest = SAFFL == "Y", arg_var_rest = ARM == "Xanomeline High Dose", arg_lbl = "pct" ) [1] "33.1%" Example 6 — Return count and percentage together fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_fl_rest = SAFFL == "Y", arg_var_rest = ARM == "Xanomeline High Dose", arg_lbl = "nbr-pct" ) [1] "84 (33.1%)" Example 7 — Compound conditions and descriptive framing Filter arguments accept any logical expression, including compound conditions with &. fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_text_desc = "The study population included ", arg_text_end = " female participants.", arg_fl_rest = SEX == "F" ) [1] "The study population included 143 female participants." Example 8 — Study completers at multiple time points Chain calls with paste() to build a multi-sentence summary. paste( fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_text_desc = "At week 8, the number of completers were: ", arg_fl_rest = COMP8FL == "Y" ), fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_text_desc = "At week 16, the number of completers were: ", arg_fl_rest = COMP16FL == "Y" ), fct_smpl_rest( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_text_desc = "At week 24, the number of completers were: ", arg_fl_rest = COMP24FL == "Y" ), sep = " " ) [1] "At week 8, the number of completers were: 190 At week 16, the number of completers were: 147 At week 24, the number of completers were: 118" 6.2 fct_var_text() 6.2.1 Purpose fct_var_text() creates a formatted text description of the distribution of a categorical variable. It counts how often each level appears, computes percentages, and returns a sentence listing the categories — connected with commas and “and” before the last item. This is ideal for: Race and sex distributions in demographics sections Discontinuation reasons in disposition sections Any categorical variable where a compact ranked summary is needed 6.2.2 Parameters Parameter Type Default Description arg_text_desc character "" Prefix text prepended to the output arg_dataset data frame — Dataset containing the variable arg_fl_rest expression NULL Optional filter applied before analysis arg_var_rest unquoted name — Categorical variable to analyse arg_order logical FALSE If TRUE, sort categories by descending frequency arg_cvt_stg function I Transformation applied to category labels (e.g., str_to_sentence) arg_nbr_obs numeric Inf Maximum number of categories to include arg_lbl character "pct" Format: "nbr", "pct", or "nbr-pct" 6.2.3 Examples Example 1 — Counts only fct_var_text( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "nbr" ) [1] "AMERICAN INDIAN OR ALASKA NATIVE (n=1), BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN (n=23) and WHITE (n=230)" Example 2 — Percentages only (default) fct_var_text( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "pct" ) [1] "AMERICAN INDIAN OR ALASKA NATIVE (0.4%), BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN (9.1%) and WHITE (90.6%)" Example 3 — Counts and percentages combined fct_var_text( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "nbr-pct" ) [1] "AMERICAN INDIAN OR ALASKA NATIVE (n=1; 0.4%), BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN (n=23; 9.1%) and WHITE (n=230; 90.6%)" Example 4 — Add a descriptive prefix fct_var_text( arg_text_desc = "The study population comprised", arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "pct" ) [1] "The study population comprised AMERICAN INDIAN OR ALASKA NATIVE (0.4%), BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN (9.1%) and WHITE (90.6%)" Example 5 — Convert labels to sentence case Raw dataset values are often uppercase. arg_cvt_stg applies any string-transformation function to the labels. fct_var_text( arg_text_desc = "The study population comprised", arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "pct", arg_cvt_stg = stringr::str_to_sentence ) [1] "The study population comprised American indian or alaska native (0.4%), Black or african american (9.1%) and White (90.6%)" Example 6 — Sort by frequency, most common and capitalised per words fct_var_text( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "pct", arg_order = TRUE, arg_cvt_stg = stringr::str_to_title ) [1] "White (90.6%), Black Or African American (9.1%) and American Indian Or Alaska Native (0.4%)" Example 7 — Limit to top 2 categories and capitalized words Combine arg_order = TRUE with arg_nbr_obs to report only the most frequent categories. fct_var_text( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "pct", arg_order = TRUE, arg_nbr_obs = 2, arg_cvt_stg = stringr::str_to_title ) [1] "White (90.6%) and Black Or African American (9.1%)" Example 8 — Filter to a specific population first and first word capitalized Percentages are computed within the filtered population. Here the safety flag makes no difference since all subjects have SAFFL == "Y", but the pattern is useful when subsets differ. fct_var_text( arg_text_desc = "Among the safety population, most were", arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_fl_rest = SAFFL == "Y", arg_var_rest = RACE, arg_lbl = "pct", arg_order = TRUE, arg_nbr_obs = 3, arg_cvt_stg = stringr::str_to_sentence ) [1] "Among the safety population, most were White (90.6%), Black or african american (9.1%) and American indian or alaska native (0.4%)" Example 9 — Discontinuation reasons (complete example) fct_var_text( arg_text_desc = "The most common reasons for treatment discontinuation were:", arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_fl_rest = DISCONFL == "Y", arg_var_rest = DCREASCD, arg_order = TRUE, arg_nbr_obs = 3, arg_cvt_stg = stringr::str_to_lower, arg_lbl = "nbr-pct" ) [1] "The most common reasons for treatment discontinuation were: adverse event (n=92; 63.9%), withdrew consent (n=27; 18.8%) and sponsor decision (n=7; 4.9%)" 6.3 fct_var_text_group() 6.3.1 Purpose fct_var_text_group() extends fct_var_text() by adding a per-group breakdown. For each category of the variable of interest it reports the overall percentage across all subjects and the within-group percentage for each level of a grouping variable (e.g. treatment arm). The output format for each category is: X% category (A% on Group1, B% on Group2, ...) This is especially useful for: Discontinuation reasons broken down by treatment arm Adverse event terms reported per treatment group Any categorical variable where between-group differences matter 6.3.2 Parameters Parameter Type Default Description arg_text_desc character "" Prefix text prepended to the output arg_dataset data frame — Dataset containing the variables arg_fl_rest expression NULL Optional filter applied before analysis arg_var_rest unquoted name — Categorical variable to summarise arg_group_var unquoted name — Grouping variable (e.g., treatment arm) arg_group_vals character vector NULL Subset of group values to include; NULL = all groups arg_group_lbl character vector NULL Custom display labels for groups (must match arg_group_vals order) arg_order logical TRUE If TRUE, order categories by descending overall frequency arg_cvt_stg function I Transformation applied to category labels (e.g., tolower) arg_nbr_obs numeric Inf Maximum number of categories to include 6.3.3 It calculates a measure of central tendency (mean or median) together with a measure of dispersion (standard deviation or range), both overall and optionally per treatment arm. 6.4.2 Parameters Parameter Type Default Description arg_dataset data frame — Dataset containing the numeric variable arg_grp unquoted name — Grouping variable (e.g., ARM, TRT01A) arg_trt_inc character vector NULL Treatment groups for the per-arm breakdown; NULL = overall total only arg_var_num unquoted name — Numeric variable to summarise (e.g., AGE, WEIGHTBL) arg_var1 character "mean" Central tendency: "mean" or "median" arg_var2 character "sd" Dispersion: "sd" (standard deviation) or "range" (min, max) arg_unit character "" Unit appended to each value (e.g., "years", "kg") arg_label character "" Variable description used in the output sentence arg_cvt_stg function I Transformation applied to sentence connectors 6.4.3 Examples Example 1 — Overall mean age with standard deviation Without arg_trt_inc, only the total across all arms is reported. fct_bsl_stats( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_var_num = AGE, arg_var1 = "mean", arg_var2 = "sd", arg_unit = "years", arg_label = "age" ) [1] "For age the overall mean was 75.1 years (SD 8.2)" Example 2 — Overall median age with range fct_bsl_stats( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_var_num = AGE, arg_var1 = "median", arg_var2 = "range", arg_unit = "years", arg_label = "age" ) [1] "For age the overall median was 77 years (range: 51, 89)" Example 3 — Mean age broken down by treatment arm Pass the arm names to arg_trt_inc to append per-arm statistics after the overall total. fct_bsl_stats( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_trt_inc = c("Xanomeline Low Dose", "Xanomeline High Dose"), arg_var_num = AGE, arg_var1 = "mean", arg_var2 = "sd", arg_unit = "years", arg_label = "age" ) [1] "For age the overall mean was 75.1 years (SD 8.2), for Xanomeline Low Dose the mean was 75.7 years (SD 8.3), and for Xanomeline High Dose the mean was 74.4 years (SD 7.9)" Example 4 — Median baseline weight with range by arm fct_bsl_stats( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_trt_inc = c("Placebo", "Xanomeline Low Dose", "Xanomeline High Dose"), arg_var_num = WEIGHTBL, arg_var1 = "median", arg_var2 = "range", arg_unit = "kg", arg_label = "baseline weight" ) [1] "For baseline weight the overall median was 66.7 kg (range: 34, 108), for Placebo the median was 60.5 kg (range: 34, 86.2), for Xanomeline Low Dose the median was 64.9 kg (range: 45.4, 106.1), and for Xanomeline High Dose the median was 69.2 kg (range: 41.7, 108)" Example 5 — Mean baseline BMI using TRT01A as the grouping variable Any treatment variable present in the dataset can serve as arg_grp. fct_bsl_stats( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = TRT01A, arg_trt_inc = c("Xanomeline High Dose", "Xanomeline Low Dose"), arg_var_num = BMIBL, arg_var1 = "mean", arg_var2 = "sd", arg_unit = "kg/m²", arg_label = "baseline BMI", arg_cvt_stg = stringr::str_to_lower ) [1] "for baseline BMI the overall mean was 24.7 kg/m² (SD 4.1), for Xanomeline High Dose the mean was 25.3 kg/m² (SD 4.2), and for Xanomeline Low Dose the mean was 25.1 kg/m² fct_bsl_stats( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_var_num = AGE, arg_var1 = "median", arg_var2 = "range", arg_unit = "years", arg_label = "age" ) %c&% fct_bsl_stats( arg_dataset = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_trt_inc = c("Xanomeline High Dose", "Xanomeline Low Dose", "Placebo"), arg_var_num = BMIBL, arg_var1 = "mean", arg_var2 = "sd", arg_unit = "kg/m²", arg_label = "baseline BMI", arg_cvt_stg = stringr::str_to_lower ) [1] "For age the overall median was 77 years (range: 51, 89) and for baseline BMI the overall mean was 24.7 kg/m² (SD 4.1), for Xanomeline High Dose the mean was 25.3 kg/m² (SD 4.2), for Xanomeline Low Dose the mean was 25.1 kg/m² (SD 4.3), and for Placebo the mean was 23.6 kg/m² (SD 3.7)" 6.5 fct_mst_aes() 6.5.1 Purpose fct_mst_aes() identifies the most common adverse events in a specified treatment group and returns a formatted sentence listing each event with its frequency across all groups. The function works by: Merging the AE dataset with the subject-level dataset on USUBJID Counting distinct subjects with each event per treatment group Computing frequency as a percentage of each group’s population Filtering to events that meet or exceed the threshold in the target arm Returning a publication-ready sentence with all frequencies 6.5.2 Parameters Parameter Type Default Description arg_data data frame — Adverse event dataset (e.g., tlr_adae); must include USUBJID arg_data_adsl data frame — Subject-level dataset (e.g., tlr_adsl); must include USUBJID and the grouping variable arg_grp unquoted name — Treatment group variable (e.g., ARM, TRT01A) arg_var unquoted name — AE variable to analyse (AEDECOD for preferred term, AEBODSYS for SOC) arg_fl_rest unquoted name — R expression to subset data arg_trt_flt unquoted name — Treatment arm used as the frequency threshold reference (use backticks if the name contains spaces) arg_frq numeric 15 Minimum frequency (%) in arg_trt_flt for an event to be included arg_freq_num logical TRUE If TRUE, frequencies are returned as numbers arg_rounding numeric 1 Number of decimal places 6.5.3 Examples Example 1 — Most common AEs (≥15%) by preferred term in the Xanomeline High Dose arm fct_mst_aes( arg_data = tlr_adae, arg_data_adsl = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_var = AEDECOD, arg_fl_rest = TRTEMFL == "Y", arg_trt_flt = `Xanomeline High Dose` ) [1] "The most common TEAEs with frequency ≥15% on Xanomeline High Dose were: pruritus (31% Xanomeline high dose; 25% Xanomeline low dose; 9.3% Placebo), application site pruritus (26.2% Xanomeline high dose; 26.2% Xanomeline low dose; 7% Placebo), application site erythema (17.9% Xanomeline high dose; 14.3% Xanomeline low dose; 3.5% Placebo), and erythema (16.7% Xanomeline high dose; 16.7% Xanomeline low dose; 9.3% Placebo)" Example 2 — Lower frequency threshold to include more events fct_mst_aes( arg_data = tlr_adae, arg_data_adsl = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_var = AEDECOD, arg_fl_rest = TRTEMFL == "Y", arg_trt_flt = `Xanomeline High Dose`, arg_frq = 10 ) [1] "The most common TEAEs with frequency ≥10% on Xanomeline High Dose were: pruritus (31% Xanomeline high dose; 25% Xanomeline low dose; 9.3% Placebo), application site pruritus (26.2% Xanomeline high dose; 26.2% Xanomeline low dose; 7% Placebo), application site erythema (17.9% Xanomeline high dose; 14.3% Xanomeline low dose; 3.5% Placebo), erythema (16.7% Xanomeline high dose; 16.7% Xanomeline low dose; 9.3% Placebo), dizziness (13.1% Xanomeline high dose; 9.5% Xanomeline low dose; 2.3% Placebo), rash (10.7% Xanomeline high dose; 15.5% Xanomeline low dose; 5.8% Placebo), and application site irritation (10.7% Xanomeline high dose; 10.7% Xanomeline low dose; 3.5% Placebo)" Example 3 — Higher threshold with two decimal places fct_mst_aes( arg_data = tlr_adae, arg_data_adsl = tlr_adsl, arg_grp = ARM, arg_var = AEDECOD, arg_fl_rest = TRTEMFL == "Y", arg_trt_flt = `Xanomeline High Dose`, arg_frq = 20, arg_rounding = 2 ) [1] "The most common TEAEs with frequency ≥20% on Xanomeline High Dose were: pruritus (30.95% Xanomeline high dose; 25% Xanomeline low dose; 9.3% Placebo), and application site pruritus (26.19% Xanomeline high dose; 26.19% Xanomeline low dose; 6.98% Placebo)" Example 4 — Summarise by system organ class (SOC) Replace AEDECOD with AEBODSYS for a higher-level safety overview.
